snapshots.name: The State of Nature
snapshots.subtitle: Locke's starting condition
snapshots.body: The condition Locke describes in Chapter II: a state of perfect freedom to act and dispose of property within the bounds of the law of nature, and a state of equality in which no one has more power than another. Unlike Hobbes, Locke's state of nature is not automatically a state of war.

snapshots.name: The State of War
snapshots.subtitle: When force replaces reason
snapshots.body: Distinguished sharply from the state of nature in Chapter III: a state of enmity and destruction created specifically by a settled design on another's life or liberty. Where there is no common judge on earth to appeal to, Locke says, the injured party has "no appeal but to heaven."

snapshots.name: Labour and Property
snapshots.subtitle: Locke's theory of ownership
snapshots.body: The argument of Chapter V: every man has property in his own person, and so in the labour of his body; whatever he removes from the common state of nature and mixes his labour with becomes his own, provided enough and as good is left for others.

snapshots.name: Consent and Political Society
snapshots.subtitle: How legitimate government begins
snapshots.body: Chapter VIII's account of how free, equal, independent men come to be subject to political power: only by their own consent, uniting into one community and agreeing to be bound by the determination of the majority.

snapshots.name: The Legislative Power
snapshots.subtitle: The supreme power in trust
snapshots.body: Described in Chapter XI as the first and fundamental positive law of every commonwealth: the power the community entrusts to make laws for the public good, which cannot be transferred elsewhere and which forfeits its authority if it acts against that trust.

snapshots.name: Tyranny
snapshots.subtitle: Power used beyond right
snapshots.body: Chapter XVIII's definition: the exercise of power beyond right, which no one can rightly have — using the power in hand not for the good of the people but for the ruler's own private, separate advantage.

snapshots.name: The Dissolution of Government
snapshots.subtitle: When a people may resist
snapshots.body: Chapter XIX's closing argument: the dissolution of a government — as when the legislative is altered or a ruler acts against his trust — is distinct from the dissolution of society itself, and returns to the people the right to provide for their own safety by a new legislative.

snapshots.name: Richard Hooker
snapshots.subtitle: The 'judicious Hooker'
snapshots.body: The Elizabethan theologian Locke repeatedly cites as an authority for the natural equality of men, quoting his Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity to support claims that would otherwise, Locke says, seem too radical coming only from him.

snapshots.name: Sir Robert Filmer
snapshots.subtitle: The patriarchalist Locke argues against
snapshots.body: The royalist writer whose Patriarcha argued that political authority descends by inheritance from Adam's God-given fatherly power. Locke names him directly to reject his account of freedom and paternal power as the foundation of legitimate government.

snapshots.name: Adam
snapshots.subtitle: The first man, in the paternal-power debate
snapshots.body: The biblical first man, invoked in Chapter VI in the argument over paternal power: Locke grants Adam was created with full reason and strength, but denies this gives all subsequent fathers, or any king claiming descent from him, absolute authority over their children.
